n: Does red meat cause cancer?
a: Processed meats are proven carcinogens. Red meat probably is, in large amounts. Limit it to 2–3 times a week.

n: Does meditation work?
a: Moderate improvement in anxiety, depression and pain. Consistency matters more than duration.

n: Should I tell my doctor about supplements?
a: Yes, always, and before surgery. Many interact with medicines.

n: How much melatonin should I take?
a: Start with 0.5–1 mg, 1–2 hours before bed. Larger doses often cause a heavy head in the morning without extra benefit.

n: Is melatonin safe for daily use?
a: It does not cause dependence like sleeping pills, but long-term safety has not been well studied. Small doses (0.5–1 mg) are often enough. For chronic insomnia, CBT-I comes first.

n: How do I improve my memory?
a: Sleep, exercise, social and mental activity, checking hearing and blood pressure. Rule out B12 deficiency.

n: Is hormone therapy safe in menopause?
a: For most healthy women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause, the benefits usually outweigh the risks. The decision is individual.

n: Are there natural remedies for hot flushes?
a: Phytoestrogens have a small benefit and black cohosh probably none. Cognitive behavioural therapy and non-hormonal medicines are alternatives.

n: Does metabolism slow with age?
a: A large study (Science 2021) showed it stays stable from 20 to 60. Muscle loss and moving less matter more.

n: Why check B12 if I take metformin?
a: Long-term metformin reduces B12 absorption and can cause neuropathy. Test once a year.

n: Why does magnesium give me diarrhoea?
a: Oxide and citrate draw water into the gut. Try glycinate or a smaller, split dose.

n: Which form of magnesium is best?
a: Glycinate is gentle on the gut and preferred for sleep. Citrate is well absorbed and helps constipation. Oxide is poorly absorbed and acts mainly as a laxative.

n: When should I take magnesium?
a: Many people take it in the evening for sleep. Keep it 2 hours apart from some antibiotics and 4 hours from thyroxine.

n: Can I take magnesium and zinc together?
a: Yes, at usual doses. Very high doses of zinc (over 40 mg) lower copper.

n: Which supplements help migraine?
a: Magnesium, riboflavin (B2) 400 mg and possibly Q10 for prevention, with results after 2–3 months.

n: Is exercise better in the morning or evening?
a: The best time is the one you can stick to. Hard exercise very close to bedtime makes sleep harder for some people.

n: I have an MTHFR mutation. Do I need methylfolate?
a: The variant is very common and most people respond normally to folic acid. Methylfolate is an alternative, not a necessity.

n: Do I need a multivitamin?
a: If you eat a varied diet, usually not. Useful with a restricted diet, older age or after bariatric surgery. It did not prevent heart disease in large studies.

n: Can I build muscle after 60?
a: Yes. Weight training increases strength and muscle at any age, together with enough protein.

n: Why do my nails break?
a: Often from water and detergents. Check iron and thyroid. Biotin only helps with a deficiency.

n: Are afternoon naps bad?
a: A 10–20 minute nap before 3 pm helps. Longer naps disrupt night-time sleep.

n: If it's natural, is it safe?
a: Not necessarily. Kava, black cohosh and green tea extract have caused liver damage, and St John's wort interacts with many medicines.

n: Is time in nature good for you?
a: 120 minutes a week is linked with better wellbeing.

n: Do nootropics work?
a: Caffeine with theanine has a small proven effect. Most others have very little data.

n: Do nuts make you fat?
a: A handful a day is not linked with weight gain in studies, despite the calories.

n: Can I cook with olive oil?
a: Yes. Virgin olive oil is stable at home cooking temperatures.

n: Omega-3 gives me fishy burps. What do I do?
a: Take them with food, try frozen or enteric-coated capsules, or the triglyceride form.

n: How much omega-3 do I need?
a: For general health 250–500 mg EPA+DHA, which 2 portions of oily fish a week provide. Higher doses (2–4 g) for triglycerides, with a doctor.

n: How do I read an omega-3 label?
a: What matters is EPA+DHA per dose, not the capsule weight. A 1000 mg capsule may contain only 300 mg EPA+DHA.

n: Is organic food healthier?
a: It has fewer pesticide residues, but no meaningful health difference has been proven. Eating more fruit and vegetables matters more.

n: Do I need calcium for my bones?
a: Get it from food first (dairy, sardines, tahini). A supplement if your diet falls short, up to 500 mg per dose.

n: Which exercise is good for the bones?
a: Weight-bearing and impact exercise (walking, stair climbing, gentle jumps if allowed). Swimming does not load the bones enough.

n: Is coffee to blame for palpitations?
a: Sometimes, especially at high doses and with energy drinks. Palpitations with chest pain or fainting need urgent assessment.

n: Does inositol help polycystic ovaries?
a: Studies show improvement in cycles and insulin. Weight loss and exercise remain the foundation.

n: What helps period pain?
a: A hot water bottle, anti-inflammatory painkillers and gentle exercise. Ginger has small positive studies. Pain that gets worse needs checking for endometriosis.

n: What helps premenstrual syndrome?
a: Exercise, calcium, vitamin B6 (up to 100 mg) and chasteberry (vitex). With severe mental symptoms, see a doctor.

n: Is bad posture to blame for neck pain?
a: The link is weaker than people think. Movement breaks and strengthening help more.

n: Do antacids affect vitamins?
a: Long-term use lowers B12, magnesium, calcium and iron. Discuss whether you still need the medicine.

n: Which supplements are safe in pregnancy?
a: Folic acid, iodine, vitamin D and iron if needed. Most herbs have no safety data. Avoid high-dose vitamin A.

n: Are pre-workouts safe?
a: They often contain very high caffeine and sometimes banned stimulants. Take care if you have arrhythmias or high blood pressure.

n: Should I take a probiotic with antibiotics?
a: It reduces diarrhoea from antibiotics. S. boulardii can be taken at the same time, bacterial strains 2 hours after.

n: How do I choose a probiotic?
a: Choose a strain studied for your problem: e.g. S. boulardii or LGG with antibiotics. Billions of CFU alone say little.

n: Does anything help the prostate?
a: Saw palmetto showed no benefit in large studies. Urinary symptoms need a urologist.

n: Does a lot of protein harm the kidneys?
a: No harm has been found in healthy kidneys. With chronic kidney disease the nephrologist sets the limit.

n: Do I need protein powder?
a: Not if you get enough protein from food. It is simply a practical source.

n: Must I take protein right after training?
a: The total daily amount matters more than the exact time. Spreading it over 3–4 meals is good practice.

n: Does diet help psoriasis?
a: Weight loss in people who are overweight improves the disease. Supplements have little benefit.

n: How do I know a supplement is good quality?
a: Look for independent certification (USP, NSF, Informed Sport), the exact form and dose on the label, and avoid "proprietary blends" and exaggerated promises. Check that it is registered with your national regulator.

n: What is the best way to quit smoking?
a: Combining counselling with medication (nicotine replacement, varenicline) gives the best chances. Public stop-smoking services are often free.

n: Will I gain weight if I quit smoking?
a: Often 3–5 kilos, but the health benefit is far greater. Exercise and fruit snacks help.

n: What helps heartburn?
a: Smaller meals, no food for 3 hours before bed, raising the head of the bed, weight loss. Peppermint makes it worse.

n: Does running ruin your knees?
a: In recreational runners it does not increase osteoarthritis. Increasing gradually prevents injuries.

n: How much salt is allowed?
a: Less than 5 g a day (one teaspoon), including the "hidden" salt in bread, cheese and ready meals.

n: Is the sauna good for you?
a: Observational data from Finland show fewer cardiovascular events. Drink water and no alcohol.

n: Does my phone affect my sleep?
a: Yes, the light and activity delay sleep. Turn screens off 30–60 minutes before bed.

n: Does selenium help Hashimoto's?
a: It lowers antibodies, but it has not been shown to change the course or replace thyroxine.

n: How do I sleep after a night shift?
a: Sunglasses on the way home, a dark and cool room, caffeine only at the start of the shift.

n: Is sitting a lot really that bad?
a: Yes, but 60–75 minutes of moderate activity a day offsets the risk.

n: What helps skin health?
a: Sunscreen, quitting smoking, sleep and moisturising. Topical retinoids have the best evidence against ageing.

n: Which supplement helps sleep most?
a: None is as effective as changing habits: a fixed schedule, morning light, less caffeine and alcohol. Melatonin helps with jet lag and falling asleep.

n: How many hours of sleep do I need?
a: Most adults need 7–9. A steady schedule is just as important.

n: What can I do about snoring?
a: Weight loss, sleeping on your side, no alcohol in the evening. With pauses in breathing, a sleep study.

n: Does loneliness affect health?
a: Yes. Strong social ties are linked with about 50% greater survival.

n: Is soy safe?
a: Yes, in normal amounts, even for women with a history of breast cancer and for men.

n: Is sparkling water bad for you?
a: No, it is safe for most people. It may cause bloating in some.

n: Does spinach have a lot of iron?
a: It has iron but little is absorbed because of oxalates. Lemon helps a little.

n: Do I need Q10 if I take a statin?
a: Statins lower Q10, but studies on muscle pain are conflicting. First discuss a change of dose or medicine with your doctor.

n: How many steps a day do I need?
a: The mortality benefit levels off at about 6,000–8,000 steps after 60 and 8,000–10,000 in younger people. Every extra step counts.

n: Why is St John's wort dangerous?
a: It reduces the effect of many medicines (contraceptives, anticoagulants, antiretrovirals) and with antidepressants it causes serotonin syndrome.

n: What helps anxiety quickly?
a: Slow breathing with a long exhale for 5 minutes, a short walk and less caffeine. For chronic anxiety, psychotherapy.
